He has a history of alcohol, benzodiazepine, heroin, and cocaine abuse. The patient has been using "anything | can get my hands on" because his depression is unbearable. stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the office for a routine visit. He has no medical problems and started preschool 3 weeks ago. The mother is concerned about his adjustment to school as he wants to stay home like his baby sister, frequently takes a long time to get dressed, and becomes upset when dropped off at school. On the first day of school, she was embarrassed when her son stomped his feet, yelled, "Take me home," and wrapped his arms around her legs, physically preventing her from leaving the classroom. The teacher reports that the boy settles down a few minutes after the mother leaves. He is shy but plays with the other children and participates in all class activities. The boy's sleep and appetite are normal, although he refuses to eat anything with peas in it. His growth and developmental milestones are within normal range. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for the boy's behavior?

stem: A 35-year-old man with a history of bipolar disorder since age 27 comes to the office for follow-up. The patient was hospitalized 2 years ago for a manic episode and was discharged with a therapeutic dose of lithium; he continues to take the same dose and is engaged in weekly psychotherapy. The patient says, "This is the best I've felt in years; work is going great, and I'm getting married in a few months. | really don't want to get hospitalized again, but | also don't want to keep taking medication if | don't have to." Prior medication trials include quetiapine and olanzapine with fluoxetine; both treatments were discontinued due to weight gain. Medical history is noncontributory. Vital signs and physical examination are unremarkable. The patient appears euthymic and has a full range of affect. Complete blood count, basic metabolic panel, and TSH are within normal limits; serum lithium level is within therapeutic range. Which of the following is the most appropriate response to this patient?

options.A: "Mood episodes are often triggered by stress or change; let's continue the medication for now and begin tapering it after your wedding."
options.B: "Mood episodes in bipolar disorder are highly recurrent; | suggest continuing lithium at the current dose and monitoring for side effects."
options.C: "Since you have had no mood episodes in the past 2 years and you meet regularly for therapy, it would | be reasonable to decrease your dose."
options.D: "We can try switching to a medication that you don't have to take daily; let's talk about the available | long-acting injectable treatments."

explanations.A: (Choice A) Because bipolar disorder is a highly recurrent illness, tapering off medication is not recommended.
explanations.B: i 66% 03 secs A 05/03/2021 Bipolar disorder is a highly recurrent illness, and multiple mood episodes are typical. The goal of maintenance treatment is to decrease the risk for recurrent manic and depressive episodes that can severely impair functioning and relationships. Lithium is a first-line agent that has been studied extensively and helps decrease rates of relapse in patients with bipolar disorder. Discontinuing stable lithium treatment usually leads to a recurrent episode within months to a year and carries risks of hospitalization, economic losses, and suicide. Understanding the patient's reasons for not wanting to be on medication and responding to any specific concerns he has about lithium are important. However, treatment recommendations must take into account the high risk of recurrent episodes. This patient is doing well on a therapeutic dose of lithium (ie, no recurrent manic or depressive episodes since starting lithium 2 years ago) and is tolerating the medication without difficulty. His medication history indicates that other treatment options (ie, quetiapine, olanzapine with fluoxetine) resulted in unacceptable weight gain. stem: A 24-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his wife due to bizarre behavior. She noticed a change in his behavior shortly after he started a fasting diet 4-5 days ago. He has become irritable and moody and has been snapping at his wife and children. The patient says that he is being haunted by large, shadowy figures that "come from another world and are trying to take me with them." He has anxiety, is sleeping less than usual, and has stopped going to work. The patient also has abdominal pain, constipation, and a tingling sensation in his fingertips. Medical history includes major depression and gastroesophageal reflux disease. His father also suffered from unexplained psychiatric episodes. The patient does not use tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drugs. His medications include omeprazole and acetaminophen. Temperature is 36.7 C (98.1 F), blood pressure is 140/80 mm Hg, pulse is 110/min, and respirations are 16/min. The abdomen is soft, bowel sounds are decreased, and there is no rebound tenderness or rigidity. Neurologic examination is within normal limits except for decreased sensation in the fingertips and mild weakness in the right arm. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?

options.C: Major depressive episode with psychotic features |

explanations.A: 66% 02 secs H+ 08/29/2021 Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP), an autosomal dominant disorder involving alterations in enzymes involved in heme biosynthesis, is characterized by acute, intermittent neurovisceral attacks. New onset of psychiatric and neurologic abnormalities following a period of fasting, accompanied by unexplained, acute abdominal pain and a family history of similar episodic symptoms, is strongly suggestive of AIP. Elevated urinary porphobilinogen levels during an attack are diagnostic. The mechanism by which AIP affects the nervous system is not fully understood but is likely related to differences in expression of the altered enzymes; common precipitants of attacks include fasting (carbohydrate restriction induces enzyme synthesis), certain medications (eg, carbamazepine, phenytoin, rifampin), tobacco, and alcohol. Abdominal pain, the most common symptom in AIP, is neuropathic; therefore, abdominal tenderness in response to direct palpation is frequently absent on physical examination. Other clinical manifestations include vomiting, constipation, sensory and motor neuropathies (eg, decreased sensation in fingertips), and tachycardia. Psychiatric symptoms may be nonspecific and include anxiety, insomnia, restlessness, mood fluctuations, and psychotic symptoms (eg, hallucinations, delusions). Acute symptoms may last for days to weeks and usually resolve between attacks. The age of onset is typically in the 20s or 30s.
explanations.B: (Choice B) Early findings in Lyme disease include erythema migrans, nonspecific systemic symptoms, and carditis, with arthritic symptoms occurring later. Common neurologic manifestations of Lyme disease include radiculopathies, meningitis, and cranial neuropathies (eg, facial palsy). Abdominal pain and psychosis are rare.
explanations.C: (Choice C) Although this patient has a history of major depressive disorder, diagnosis of a recurrent major depressive episode requires a 2-week duration and cannot be made when a patient's presentation is better explained by a medical illness (as in this patient with classic symptoms of AIP).
explanations.D: (Choice D) Schizophrenia is characterized by psychotic symptoms that have persisted for at least 6 months and are not better explained by a medical condition.
explanations.E: (Choice E) Wilson disease leads to copper accumulation in tissues, causing insidious onset of hepatic, psychiatric, and neurologic dysfunction. Abdominal pain in Wilson disease is generally due to acute hepatitis or liver failure (eg, jaundice, right upper quadrant pain). Neurologic findings typically affect movement (eg, dysarthria, dystonia, tremor, parkinsonism) and are almost always accompanied by corneal copper deposits (Kayser-Fleischer rings).
